why: Looking at fingerprint patterns, how ridges form and how hidden prints show up helps your child compare patterns and explain evidence.
teaser: Find loops, whorls and arches, then go deeper: prints made before birth, koala prints, and wrinkly bath fingers.
title: Fingerprints Up Close
question: What are fingerprints, and why do we have them?
idea: Fingertips have tiny ridges that leave a pattern of sweat and oil. The pattern forms before birth, may help us feel fine textures, and no two have ever been found to match.

curiosity.intro: Start with the basics: three patterns and a hidden print. Then go deep into how ridges form and what they might do.
curiosity.carryForward: Look for the pattern, then look closer for the tiny ridge details.

questions.question: Is your print a loop, a whorl or an arch?
questions.notice: Find the three prints. One has ridges that curve back, one has a circle, and one has a small hill in the middle.
questions.say: A loop has ridges that come in and curve back out the same side. A whorl has circles or a spiral. An arch has ridges that flow across with a bump in the middle. Loops are the most common, and arches are the rarest.
questions.try: Rub a pencil hard on paper to make a dark gray patch. Press one fingertip on it. Press clear tape on your fingertip, peel it off, and stick it on white paper. Is your print a loop, a whorl or an arch?

questions.question: What tiny details are inside a print?
questions.notice: Find a ridge that stops, and a ridge that splits in two. Look for the tiny dots along the top of the ridges.
questions.say: Sweat pores sit in a row along the top of each ridge. Experts look at minutiae, the tiny places where a ridge ends or splits in two. A split is called a bifurcation. They compare these points, not just the pattern. Very rarely, a change in a gene called SMARCAD1 means a person is born with no fingerprints at all.
questions.try: Look at your tape print with a magnifying glass if you have one. Find one place where a ridge ends. Then find one place where a ridge splits in two.

questions.question: Why does a koala have fingerprints?
questions.notice: Look at the koala's hand holding the branch. Find the tips of its fingers.
questions.say: Koala prints look very much like ours. But koalas are only distantly related to us, and their cousins, wombats and kangaroos, do not have prints. Scientists think prints formed separately in both because both grip and handle things.
questions.try: Draw a koala hand holding a branch. Then trace your own hand next to it. Tell one way they are alike.

questions.question: Why do fingers get wrinkly in the bath?
questions.notice: Find the two bowls, the wet marbles, and the bowl of water.
questions.say: Wrinkly bath fingers are not just skin soaking up water. Your nerves control them. Tiny blood vessels under the skin get narrower, and the skin puckers. Scientists think wrinkles might help us grip wet things, but studies disagree, so for now we say maybe.
questions.try: Time how fast you move wet marbles from one bowl to another with dry fingers. Soak your hands in warm water until they wrinkle, then try again. This is a fun try, not proof.

reading.title: Fingerprints, then deeper
reading.coverText: Start with three patterns and a hidden print. Then go deep: prints before birth, koala prints and wrinkly fingers.
reading.parentNote: Age 8 with a stretch. Welcome spoken answers, pointing, drawing and dictation.
reading.foldableNote: Carry six fingerprint clues in a small book.

beats.title: A hidden print
beats.passage: Little held up a glass. "I don't see anything," Little said. Big tipped it to the light. A faint print showed up. Your fingertips have tiny ridges. The ridges carry a thin film of sweat and oil. When you touch something, the film copies the ridge pattern. Most prints are latent, which means hidden until someone makes them show.
beats.prompt: Why can a fingertip leave a print on a glass?

foldable.heading: A hidden print
foldable.body: Tiny ridges carry sweat and oil. A touch copies their pattern, even when you cannot see it.

beats.title: Three patterns
beats.passage: Most prints belong to one of three pattern families. In a loop, ridges come in and curve back out the same side. In a whorl, ridges make circles or a spiral. In an arch, ridges flow across with a bump in the middle. Loops are the most common. Arches are the rarest. No two prints have ever been found to match, not even on identical twins.
beats.prompt: How is a loop different from an arch?

foldable.heading: Three patterns
foldable.body: Loops curve back. Whorls make circles. Arches flow across with a bump. No two have ever been found to match.

beats.title: Made before birth
beats.passage: Prints form before a baby is born. At about 7 to 8 weeks of growing, puffy pads appear on the fingertips. At about 10 to 11 weeks, ridges start to form. By about 15 to 17 weeks, the pattern is set. Twins get different prints because each fingertip grows in its own tiny way. After that, the pattern normally just grows bigger and keeps its shape, though a deep cut or some skin diseases can leave a scar.
beats.prompt: Why do identical twins have different prints?

foldable.heading: Made before birth
foldable.body: Prints form before birth. Each fingertip grows in its own tiny way, so even twins differ.

beats.title: Koala prints
beats.passage: Koalas have prints that look very much like ours. Koalas are only distantly related to us, and their cousins, wombats and kangaroos, have none. Scientists think prints formed separately in both because both grip things. What are ridges for? In one lab test, ridges made the shakes from rubbing a fine texture much stronger. So scientists think ridges help us feel fine textures.
beats.prompt: Why do scientists think both koalas and people have prints?

foldable.heading: Koala prints
foldable.body: Koalas and people both grip things. Scientists think ridges may help us feel fine textures.

beats.title: A safe print lift
beats.passage: Detectives make hidden prints show up in a lab. They dust powder, use a chemical called ninhydrin that turns prints purple, or use superglue fumes. Those are jobs for trained lab workers, not for kids. Little and Big made a safe one. They rubbed a pencil on paper, pressed a fingertip on it, and lifted the print with clear tape. Big found a spot where a ridge split in two.
beats.prompt: How did Little and Big make a print show up safely?

foldable.heading: A safe print lift
foldable.body: Detective tools are for trained lab workers. A pencil patch and clear tape make a safe print.

beats.title: Wrinkly fingers
beats.passage: After a long bath, fingers get wrinkly. Your nerves cause it. Blood vessels under the skin get narrower, and the skin puckers. Fingers with cut nerves do not wrinkle. Maybe the wrinkles help us grip wet things, like treads on a tire. One study found people moved wet marbles faster with wrinkly fingers. Another found no difference. So for now, we say maybe.
beats.prompt: Why is the answer about wrinkly fingers still maybe?

foldable.heading: Wrinkly fingers
foldable.body: Nerves make bath fingers wrinkle. Maybe wrinkles help grip wet things. Scientists are still checking.

yourTurn.title: Your turn
yourTurn.prompt: Make a pencil-and-tape print. Write one sentence about its pattern.
yourTurn.example: Example: My print is a loop because the ridges curve back out the same side.

math.title: Fingerprint counts
math.intro: Compare and round pretend counts from a fingerprint notebook.

tasks.prompt: Little counts 38 ridges on one print and 52 ridges on another. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater count (or the shared count if equal)?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. When both counts match, use = and give that shared count.
tasks.worked: 38 < 52. Compare the tens first, so the greater count is 52.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big presses 71 prints on one page and 67 prints on the next page. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater count (or the shared count if equal)?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. When both counts match, use = and give that shared count.
tasks.worked: 71 > 67. Compare the tens first, so the greater count is 71.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Little finds 45 pores on one strip of tape and 45 pores on another. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater count (or the shared count if equal)?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. When both counts match, use = and give that shared count.
tasks.worked: 45 = 45. Both counts match, so the shared count is 45.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Big counts 34 ridge endings on a big drawing. What is 34 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones. With 5 or more, go up to the next ten; otherwise go down.
tasks.worked: 34 has 4 ones, so round down to 30.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Little draws 86 tiny pore dots. What is 86 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones. With 5 or more, go up to the next ten; otherwise go down.
tasks.worked: 86 has 6 ones, so round up to 90.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Big moves 65 wet marbles in a long game. What is 65 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones. With 5 or more, go up to the next ten; otherwise go down.
tasks.worked: 65 has 5 ones, so round up to 70.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one problem and draw the tens as sticks and the ones as dots to check.
math.printNote: Show your thinking with numbers, marks, or words.
math.parentNote: Three two-digit comparisons and three nearest-ten roundings. The numbers are for practice, not real fingerprint counts.
math.answerKeyIntro: Compare tens first, then ones. For rounding, 5 or more ones rounds up.

writing.intro: Choose one picture. Say your idea first, then draw or write it.
writing.draw: Draw your own fingerprint big. Mark one place where a ridge ends or splits.

frames.start: My print is a loop, whorl or arch because

writing.check: Does your sentence tell what you noticed and use because or maybe to explain?
writing.parentNote: Offer dictation: let the child say a complete thought while you write it, then invite a picture or label.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Ridges carry a thin film of sweat and oil, and a touch copies the ridge pattern onto the glass. Most prints are latent, or hidden.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Prints form before birth (pads at about 7 to 8 weeks, ridges at about 10 to 11, set by about 15 to 17). Each fingertip grows in its own tiny way, so twins differ.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: Scientists think ridges help us feel fine textures, and maybe wrinkles help grip wet things. Studies on wrinkles disagree, so for now we say maybe.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a spoken, dictated, drawn, or written sentence about one fingerprint clue.

parentGuidance: No two prints have ever been found to match (not a proof). Weeks count from when growth starts (pregnancy weeks run about 2 higher). Twins differ because each fingertip pad grows differently. Scientists think ridges help us feel fine textures; the grip idea is unsettled. Adermatoglyphia, a very rare SMARCAD1 change, means no prints from birth. Powder, ninhydrin and superglue fuming are adult lab work only; kids use pencil graphite and tape. Stay nearby for the wet-marble try and use warm, not hot, water.

questions.answer: Arches are the rarest. Loops are the most common.
Prints form before birth, and the pattern is set by about 15 to 17 weeks of growing.
Koalas. Their cousins, kangaroos and wombats, do not have prints.
Your nerves narrow the blood vessels under the skin, and the skin puckers.

poem.title: Little Wonderer Leaves Clues
lines: Little Wonderer touched the jam jar lid,
the window, the doorknob, the drum. Yes, it did.
It patted the mirror, it poked at the cake,
it tapped every spoon just for tapping’s sake.
“Oh no!” Little cried. “There are clues everywhere!
A loop on the cupboard! A whorl on the chair!
A detective could follow my trail through the house.
I’m as easy to find as a jam-covered mouse!”
Big Wonderer nodded and wiped off a pane.
“Your swirls will grow bigger but mostly remain.
No two have been found to match, pair after pair,
so a print is a clue that says someone was there.”
So Little wore socks on both hands for the day,
to tiptoe through mischief and sneak right away.
But it tripped on the rug and it fell in the dough,
and now there’s a Little-shaped print, head to toe.

drawing.alt: A black-ink drawing of Little Wonderer, with socks on its hands, sitting beside a Little-shaped imprint in bread dough on a kitchen table while Big Wonderer looks on.
